correctness.rationale: For separated platforms with a finite set of active cost atoms, each contributing vote mass is a strictly increasing voter-CDF function of the sum of platform positions. A sufficiently small move toward the opponent preserves the active cost set and strictly improves the left candidate payoff, excluding all positive-turnout equilibria. For inactive profiles, endpoint deviations show that a fixed opponent admits no profitable deviation exactly when its position lies in \([0,1]\cap[1-c_*,c_*]\). The resulting square gives both necessity and sufficiency including \(c_*=0,1/2,1\). The discrete empirical-CDF discrepancy is exactly \(1/(m+1)\), its left-limit participation probabilities obey the same bound, and the limiting uniform-cost quartile profile is checked by global quadratic best-response maxima. Uniform payoff convergence and the \(2/(m+1)\) approximate-equilibrium estimate follow analytically. A standalone exact-arithmetic checker supports algebraic boundary checks but is not used as a proof of infinite claims.

originality.rationale: The closest September 2026 research derives polarized equilibria for a continuous cost-density model; the new theorem gives the complete pure-equilibrium set for every finite cost spectrum, any atomless full-support electorate, and demonstrates loss of exact equilibrium under uniformly convergent payoff approximations. Its step-CDF hypotheses do not satisfy the density assumptions of the published existence analysis, and its no-equilibrium conclusion is incompatible with directly transferring the continuous-cost conclusion. Targeted scientific-source and research-record searches surfaced no matching finite-atom classification. The main priority risk is inaccessible complete appendices and unindexed related work; absence from search is not evidence of global novelty.
residual_risks: The complete appendix of arXiv:2609.29869v1 could not be inspected after repeated primary-document retrieval attempts.
Other older spatial-abstention papers may treat deterministic or atomic voting costs under an equivalent vote-mass objective without using this title or terminology.
Search records and titles alone cannot establish global novelty; independent publication-priority review remains to be performed.

value.rationale: Finite empirical cost spectra are a standard representation of heterogeneous voting costs in simulation and computation. This complete theorem shows that all positive-turnout pure equilibria vanish for every finite spectrum, with a sharp half-interval threshold for the remaining no-turnout cases, independent of the electorate shape or masses. Its explicit sequence of cost distributions converges in Kolmogorov distance and induces uniformly converging game payoffs yet never has a pure equilibrium, while retaining \(2/(m+1)\)-approximate equilibria. That exact-versus-approximate separation is structurally informative for numerical equilibrium inference and goes well beyond a single trivial negative case.
